# The Shockley–Ramo theorem {#sec-ramo} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/ramo.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 11–15 (induced current of a photogenerated electron–hole pair drifting between two electrodes, electron and hole transit times, total collected charge).* ## Key relations When does the external current flow: when the carriers *reach* the electrodes, or while they *move*? The Shockley–Ramo theorem answers: while they move. Consider an EHP created at $x=l$ in a semiconductor of length $L$ between two electrodes held at a voltage $V$, with a uniform field $E=V/L$ (slide 11). In a time $dt$ the electron drifts $dx=v_edt$ and the field does the work $eE\,dx$ on it. That energy comes from the battery, which supplies $Vi_e(t)dt$ (slide 12): $$ eE\,dx=Vi_e\,dt\quad\Longrightarrow\quad i_e(t)=\frac{ev_e}{L}\quad (tE = ${(rmOut.E / 1e5).toFixed(2)} kV/cm · ve = ${(rmOut.ve / 1e3).toFixed(1)} km/s, vh = ${(rmOut.vh / 1e3).toFixed(1)} km/s
te = ${(rmOut.te * 1e12).toFixed(1)} ps · th = ${(rmOut.th * 1e12).toFixed(1)} ps · charge carried by the electron ${rmOut.Qe.toFixed(2)} e, by the hole ${rmOut.Qh.toFixed(2)} e, total 1.00 e` ``` Set $l/L\to 0$: the pair is created next to the electrode the hole drifts to. The hole contributes almost nothing; the electron crosses the whole device and carries the full charge. Raise the voltage with the Si velocities on: the current pulse grows taller and shorter until the carriers reach their **saturation velocity** (about $10^5$ m/s, slide 31). Beyond that, more volts no longer buy speed. ## Many pairs: the transit-time impulse response A short light pulse creates pairs with the profile $e^{-\alpha x}$ of @sec-absorption (light entering at $x=0$, on the side where the holes are collected). The photocurrent is the sum of the rectangular pulses of all pairs. Its Fourier transform is the transit-time frequency response. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof tr = Inputs.form({ W: Inputs.range([0.5, 50], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "drift-region width W (µm)"}), la: Inputs.range([3, 8], {value: 5, step: 0.05, label: "log₁₀ absorption coefficient α (m⁻¹)"}), ve: Inputs.range([1e4, 2e5], {value: 1e5, step: 1e3, label: "electron velocity v_e (m/s)"}), vh: Inputs.range([1e4, 2e5], {value: 7e4, step: 1e3, label: "hole velocity v_h (m/s)"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false trOut = { const W = tr.W * 1e-6, a = 10 ** tr.la, tmax = 1.1 * W / Math.min(tr.ve, tr.vh), ts = d3.range(0, 501).map(i => tmax * i / 500); const r = pinImpulse(ts, W, a, tr.ve, tr.vh, 300); const pts = r.flatMap(d => [{t: d.t * 1e12, i: d.ie / qe * 1e-12, c: "electrons"}, {t: d.t * 1e12, i: d.ih / qe * 1e-12, c: "holes"}, {t: d.t * 1e12, i: (d.ie + d.ih) / qe * 1e-12, c: "total"}]); const fmax = 2 * Math.max(tr.ve, tr.vh) / W; const resp = d3.range(0, 301).map(i => { const f = fmax * i / 300; return {f: f / 1e9, H: 20 * Math.log10(Math.max(transitMag(f, W, a, tr.ve, tr.vh), 1e-6))}; }); return {pts, resp, f3: f3dB(f => transitMag(f, W, a, tr.ve, tr.vh), fmax), absorbed: 1 - Math.exp(-a * W), aW: a * W}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 250, x: {label: "time after the light pulse (ps)"}, y: {label: "current per EHP (e/ps)", grid: true}, color: {legend: true, domain: ["electrons", "holes", "total"], range: ["#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#0b0b0b"]}, marks: [Plot.line(trOut.pts, {x: "t", y: "i", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 2})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 220, x: {label: "modulation frequency (GHz)"}, y: {label: "|H_transit| (dB)", domain: [-15, 1], grid: true}, marks: [Plot.line(trOut.resp, {x: "f", y: "H", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([-3], {stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "3,3"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
αW = ${trOut.aW.toPrecision(3)} → fraction absorbed in the drift region ${(100 * trOut.absorbed).toFixed(1)} % · transit-limited bandwidth f3dB = ${(trOut.f3 / 1e9).toFixed(2)} GHz = ${(trOut.f3 * tr.W * 1e-6 / Math.min(tr.ve, tr.vh)).toFixed(2)} × vslow/W
` ``` Strong absorption ($\alpha W\gg1$) creates all pairs near $x=0$: only electrons cross the device, and the pulse lasts $W/v_e$. Weak absorption gives uniform generation: both carriers contribute, each pulse is a triangle. Because the holes are slower, it pays to generate the carriers on the side where the holes are collected. This is why fast photodiodes are lit through the p⁺ side, and why the "uni-travelling-carrier" photodiode (see Going further) lets only electrons travel. ::: {#cell-fig-ramo-response .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} f = np.linspace(0, 15e9, 1500) W, ve, vh = 10e-6, 1e5, 7e4 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6)) for a, lab in ((1e7, "αW = 100 (surface, electrons cross)"), (0, "uniform generation")): H = dl.transit_response(f, W, a, ve, vh) ax.plot(f/1e9, 20*np.log10(abs(H)), label=f"{lab}: f₃dB = {dl.f3dB(f, H)/1e9:.2f} GHz") H = dl.transit_response(f, W, 1e7, vh, ve) # swap roles: the slow carrier crosses ax.plot(f/1e9, 20*np.log10(abs(H)), "--", label=f"surface, holes cross: f₃dB = {dl.f3dB(f, H)/1e9:.2f} GHz") ax.axhline(-3, color=dl.INK2, ls=":", lw=1); ax.set(xlabel="f (GHz)", ylabel="|H| (dB)", ylim=(-15, 1)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Transit-time frequency response of a 10 µm drift region (v_e = 10⁵ m/s, v_h = 7×10⁴ m/s) for surface absorption, uniform absorption, and absorption on the wrong side (light entering where the electrons are collected, so the slow holes cross the whole device).](ramo_files/figure-html/fig-ramo-response-output-1.png){#fig-ramo-response width=728 height=374} ::: ::: For a single carrier crossing the whole width in $t_{tr}=W/v$ the pulse is a rectangle and $|H|=|\mathrm{sinc}(ft_{tr})|$, whose −3 dB point is $f_{3dB}=0.443/t_{tr}=0.443\,v/W$. Uniform generation shares the work between the two carriers and is faster for the same width. ## Worked check (slides 12–15) ::: {#tbl-ramo .cell tbl-cap='An EHP created at l = 3 µm in a 10 µm Si sample at 10 V. The two rectangular pulses carry (L − l)/L and l/L of the charge.' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} L, l, V = 10e-6, 3e-6, 10.0 ve, vh = dl.drift_velocity(V/L, "e"), dl.drift_velocity(V/L, "h") t = np.linspace(0, 2e-10, 200001) ie, ih = dl.ramo_single(t, l, L, ve, vh) Qe, Qh = np.trapezoid(ie, t), np.trapezoid(ih, t) pd.DataFrame([("field E = V/L", f"{V/L:.1e} V/m"), ("v_e, v_h (Caughey–Thomas)", f"{ve:.3g}, {vh:.3g} m/s"), ("t_e = (L − l)/v_e", f"{(L - l)/ve*1e12:.1f} ps"), ("t_h = l/v_h", f"{l/vh*1e12:.1f} ps"), ("i_e = ev_e/L, i_h = ev_h/L", f"{dl.qe*ve/L*1e9:.2f} nA, {dl.qe*vh/L*1e9:.2f} nA"), ("charge Q_e + Q_h", f"{Qe/dl.qe:.3f} e + {Qh/dl.qe:.3f} e = {(Qe + Qh)/dl.qe:.3f} e")], columns=["quantity", "value"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **The general theorem.** For any electrode geometry, a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\mathbf v$ induces on electrode $k$ the current $i_k=q\,\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf E_w$, where $\mathbf E_w$ is the **weighting field**: the field obtained with electrode $k$ at 1 V, all others grounded and all charges removed. For parallel plates $E_w=1/L$ and we recover slide 12. In an interdigitated MSM detector (@sec-schottky) $E_w$ is concentrated near the fingers: a carrier contributes most of its current when it is close to the electrode. Compute $E_w$ for a pixelated X-ray detector and explain the "small-pixel effect". - **Uni-travelling-carrier (UTC) photodiode.** Absorb the light in a thin p-doped layer, where the photogenerated holes are majority carriers and relax immediately; only electrons enter the depleted collector, at velocities up to $3\times10^5$ m/s in InP (velocity overshoot). UTC photodiodes reach > 100 GHz and high saturation currents (no hole pile-up). Use the panel with the hole velocity set very high to mimic it. - **Space charge.** At high photocurrents the drifting carriers screen the field (the photocurrent density approaches $\varepsilon v_{sat}V/W^2$) and the response saturates. Estimate this saturation current for a 20 µm diameter, 1 µm thick InGaAs pin at 3 V. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - W. Shockley, *J. Appl. Phys.* 9, 635 (1938); S. Ramo, *Proc. IRE* 27, 584 (1939) (references of slide 11). - Z. He, "Review of the Shockley–Ramo theorem and its application in semiconductor gamma-ray detectors", *Nucl. Instrum. Meth. A* 463, 250 (2001): a very readable derivation with weighting potentials. - T. Ishibashi *et al.*, "Uni-travelling-carrier photodiodes", *IEICE Trans. Electron.* E83-C, 938 (2000). ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Prove that the charge collected is $e$ for any generation point, even if $v_e$ and $v_h$ depend on position. 2. Show that $|H(f)|=|\sin(\pi ft_{tr})/(\pi ft_{tr})|$ for a single carrier and find the −3 dB frequency. 3. In the second panel, what drift-region width gives a 10 GHz transit-limited bandwidth in Si at saturation velocity? What fraction of 850 nm light ($\alpha\approx5\times10^4$ m⁻¹) does it absorb? 4. A carrier is trapped halfway across the device and never released. What charge is collected in the external circuit?
